extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, law students, and legal scholars interested in unfair-competition/equity disputes between news services
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-evidentiary criteria and equitable principles relevant to a suit seeking injunctive relief for alleged theft/piracy of news by rival press associations. Focuses on facts, industry custom, contracts/confidentiality, and equitable defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean hands / equity doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: "He that would have equity must do equity"; "He that comes into equity must come with clean hands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff who has engaged in the same wrongful conduct it seeks to enjoin may be denied equitable relief. Counsel cites authorities (e.g., Thompson) showing courts turn plaintiffs out of equity where they have pirated others; whether this bars relief depends on facts and proven conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether plaintiff engaged in same or similar wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is proven the complainant has been doing the very same things it complains of in the defendant, then it may have no standing in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine affidavits and factual proof of reciprocal practices (e.g., hiring people to 'lift' news) — if both parties engaged in similar systematic conduct the plaintiff's request for injunction is weakened or defeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual obligations and duty of members
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a press co-operative are "bound to furnish" local news to the service; conversely, members may be under obligations not to disclose news to competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a defendant is 'entitled' to tips or local news depends on the contractual relationship between the member newspaper and the press association; taking tips that constitute a breach of members' obligations to the plaintiff is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive acquisition / proprietary character of news
rubrics_metrics.description: The contention that a service receives cable/news "exclusive of any news received by The Associated Press" and pays to obtain that exclusive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates claims that certain dispatches/cable news were exclusive and obtained by payment; evidence that defendant paid for or systematically acquired exclusive material supports the plaintiff's claim of wrongful appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of employees/reporters to 'lift' news (paid tips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations and evidence that men were "regularly employed ... for the express and only purpose of lifting news" from rival services or early editions, and that individuals were paid (e.g., salaries of $3, $5, $10/week) to supply or protect news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factfinder should assess whether hiring employees or paying reporters to supply competitors' news constitutes wrongful conduct; specific affidavits (e.g., Cleveland transaction) and payroll details are relevant proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic pilfering v. isolated incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish a single subordinate's wrong (an isolated Cleveland instance) from a systematic department set up to lift news month-to-month and year-to-year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence shows an organized, repeated practice across many cities, the claim of wrongful appropriation is stronger; if only an isolated subordinate acted, defenses (lack of corporate knowledge or intent) may be viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry custom and long-standing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding custom: both press associations and newspapers have for years taken news from early editions and copied among services — described as 'the rule' since their existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider customary industry practices when judging fairness; a practice widely accepted historically may mitigate the appearance of wrongdoing, though custom does not automatically legalize wrongful acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and weight of evidence (affidavits/testimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of affidavits demonstrating specific instances (e.g., Lusitania, Pope, Jutland, Cleveland) and corroboration among witnesses (Warnock, Cochran, Cox, Baskervill, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision whether to grant injunctive relief turns on the factual record: number, specificity, corroboration, and timing of affidavits; rebuttal affidavits can change the outcome. The Court emphasizes it "comes down to the question of fact."

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of injunction on business operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an injunction would 'put you out of business' or be 'harmless' to the defendant or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh the practical economic harm an injunction would cause; defendants argue that confining them to their own collected news would be inadequate and injurious to their business model. That impact is a factor in equitable relief balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest and access to foreign/world news
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that obtaining world news despite foreign censors is in the public interest and that restricting such access may be 'not in the interest of our country or of our people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where injunctive relief would limit public access to news or require strict deference to foreign censors, courts may consider public-interest implications in balancing equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on precedent and analogous authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to cases (e.g., Thompson v. American Law Book Co., Price Manufacturing v. Prince Paint Co., a Supreme Court Holmes gambling-institution case) to determine equitable principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal outcomes depend on applying precedent about unclean hands, plaintiffs' misconduct, and equitable remedies; counsel argues for/against broad concessions based on such authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract/confidentiality arrangements with correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of 'confidential arrangement' that employees 'must not disclose our news' and purchase terms under which newspapers 'buy' service material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are explicit contractual/confidentiality obligations binding correspondents or member papers, using such news by rivals can be a breach; courts examine the terms and whether defendants induced or exploited breaches.
